idiom_name: interface declaration with default member bodies
implementation_notes: Kotlin's interface cannot store state - properties must be abstract or provide accessors without backing fields - so the language construct is this pattern exactly, and the compiler rejects any attempt to give a contract a field. Members may carry default bodies (compiled to JVM default methods), which is how contracts grow without breaking implementors, and override is mandatory so an implementation cannot silently replace a member. Use an abstract class only when the contract needs shared state or a constructor; interfaces give multiple inheritance of type, which is what lets one class promise several roles.
pitfalls: Properties in an interface cannot have backing fields (val x: Int = 0 does not compile), so what looks like contract state must be computed by an accessor or supplied by the implementation.
A class that implements two interfaces declaring the same default member must override it and resolve explicitly (super<A>.m()), so default bodies bring diamond rules back into the contract layer.
The -jvm-default compiler mode decides whether member bodies become real default methods or DefaultImpls bridges, which changes binary compatibility of published contracts across Kotlin versions.

variants.name: Sealed interface (closed contract)
variants.implementation_notes: A sealed interface may only be implemented inside the module and package that declares it, so the contract becomes a closed set of implementations and a when expression over it is checked for exhaustiveness without an else branch - the Kotlin form of an algebraic sum type. Choose it when the implementations are known and consumers must handle all cases; keep an open interface when third parties are expected to add implementations, since they cannot implement a sealed one at all.
variants.code_sketch:
sealed interface Error                        // closed contract
class FileError(val path: String) : Error
object Timeout : Error

fun message(e: Error): String = when (e) {     // exhaustive: no else
    is FileError -> "cannot read ${e.path}"
    Timeout -> "timed out"
}
pitfalls: Kotlin sealed subtypes must live in the same package and module as the contract, so a sealed interface cannot cross an expected/actual multiplatform boundary or be implemented by another module.

The closure is a compile-time and IDE guarantee: on JVM targets without PermittedSubclasses the sealed interface is compiled as an ordinary interface, so Java or bytecode-level code can still implement it.

variants.name: Functional (SAM) interface
variants.implementation_notes: A fun interface declares exactly one abstract member, and a lambda converts to it at the call site, so the contract becomes a function shape and implementations need no class at all. Use it when the role is a single operation and most implementations are ad hoc; keep a plain interface when the contract has more than one abstract member, needs a meaningful name at every call site, or must be implemented by a class with state.
pitfalls: A functional interface is a distinct type from a function type: Predicate and (Int) -> Boolean are not interchangeable without conversion, and each conversion can allocate a wrapper.
fun interfaces cannot be sealed, because their implementations are anonymous by design, so no exhaustiveness checking is available for them.
